title: The traveler who leaves no tracks
hookLine: a good traveler leaves no tracks, and the sage rejects no one (Tao Te Ching 27)
carry: the sage casts no one away
tomorrow: know the strong, keep to the soft

cards: Early morning at a lakeside campsite. The tent is down and rolled. The fire ring is cold, the stones put back where they were found.
Someone has walked the whole site once, head down, picking up a bottle cap and a twist tie that weren't even theirs.

By the time the car pulls away, the clearing looks the way it did before they came, maybe a little better. The next family will never know anyone was there. Hikers have a phrase for this: leave no trace.
Chapter twenty-seven of the Tao Te Ching says something like it, in its own way.

teach.b: First, no tracks, no tallies. In Legge's translation, the chapter opens: "The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps." Then a list in the same key.
A good speaker says nothing anyone can find fault with. A good counter needs no tally sticks. The skill is so complete you can't see the machinery.
Second, locks without bolts. A good closer shuts a door with no bolt, and still it can't be opened. A good binder ties with no rope, and still it can't be undone.
What holds things together here isn't hardware. It's something quieter, like trust, or care so thorough it doesn't need a padlock.
Third, no one thrown away. Then the chapter turns to people. The sage, it says, is good at saving people, and so no one is cast away.
Good at saving things, and so nothing is thrown out. The chapter gives this a name, which translators render in different ways; some hear in it a hidden light.
Fourth, teacher and material. The chapter ends with a pairing that can surprise. The good person is the teacher of the one who isn't good.

And the one who isn't good is the good person's material, what they have to work with. If you don't honor your teacher, and don't care for your material, the chapter says, then however clever you are, you are badly lost.

teach.h: NO TRACKS, AND NO ONE CAST AWAY.
teach.b: Leaving no tracks isn't only about tidiness. It's about doing good so quietly that nobody is rejected, and nobody is left owing.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching put chapter twenty-seven into practice through small unseen acts of care, tidying, repairing, helping, done without leaving any mark of who did them.

o: traveling alone, without any map or plan
hiding your mistakes so no one finds them
doing good so quietly it leaves no trace

s: chapter twenty-seven says the sage gives up on people who can't be helped
the sage is good at saving people, so no one is cast away.
the chapter calls the one who isn't good the good person's material
the good person is the teacher; the one who isn't good is what the good person has to work with.
in this chapter, a good closer needs a strong lock
a good closer shuts a door with no bolt, and still it can't be opened.

games.q: you're the sage of chapter twenty-seven, and someone in your town is known as a lost cause. what do you do?
o: keep them out, for everyone's sake.
save them, because the sage casts no one away.
wait for them to fix themselves.
games.why: the sage is good at saving people, and so no one is cast away. even the one who isn't good is called the good person's material.

practice: Think through the places you'll pass through today: a shared kitchen, a bus seat, a friend's couch. Pick one, and one small thing that would leave it better, a wiped counter, a straightened chair.
Picture yourself walking away from it, with nobody thanking you and nothing to show.

wordCard.voice: No tracks. Chapter twenty-seven's skilled traveler, who leaves no trace, and its sage, who throws no one away. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, shàn xíng wú zhé jì: good travel leaves no wheel tracks. The opening of Tao Te Ching 27.

carryVoice: Your line: the sage casts no one away. The finest skill hides its own machinery. That's today, done.
